summary: Describes use cases and architecture for carrying PASSporT caller identity tokens outside the call signaling path, for calls that do not use SIP end-to-end or cannot deliver headers reliably.

plainLanguage.summary: A caller ID proof is sent by a side route when the main route cannot carry it.

questions: how to verify caller identity without sip headers
what is a call placement service
how does out-of-band stir verify caller id
subtitle: How a caller's signed identity token can reach the callee through a side channel when the phone network cannot carry it.

tldr.problem: PASSporT tokens prove who is calling, but many calls cross the legacy phone network (PSTN) or other paths that cannot carry SIP headers end-to-end, so the proof gets stripped or damaged.
tldr.mechanism: The caller or a gateway encrypts the PASSporT to the callee's public key and stores it at a Call Placement Service indexed by the called number. The callee fetches and decrypts it when the call arrives.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives use cases, a broad architecture and a strawman HTTPS interface, but not a complete protocol. A real deployment would need further specification.

today: RFC 8816 is an Informational RFC from the IETF and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. The text itself says it defines use cases, an architecture and a strawman interface, and that deploying it would need additional specification.

sections.title: Why Caller Identity Needs a Side Channel
sections.content:
STIR exists to fight impersonation in the telephone network, such as illegal robocalling, voicemail hacking and swatting. RFC 8224 defines a SIP Identity header field that carries a PASSporT (RFC 8225), a signed token attesting that the caller may use the calling number.

That works only if SIP signaling survives end-to-end. Many calls start or end at PSTN endpoints, or cross the PSTN in the middle. The core PSTN elements are legacy devices unlikely to be upgraded to pass in-band signatures, and some would strip or damage them. At the same time, the endpoints (smart phones, IP PBXs, terminal adapters) are increasingly programmable and have Internet access.

Out-of-band STIR uses that gap. It is also pitched as a transitional technology while in-band STIR adoption ramps up.
sections.plainLanguage: A sealed letter that proves who you are cannot go through an old mail chute that tears letters. So you leave a copy at a pickup point, and the person you are calling goes there to collect it.

sections.title: The Call Placement Service
sections.content:
Because endpoints cannot pass cryptographic data through call signaling, the design needs a rendezvous point called a Call Placement Service (CPS). A CPS stores a record of call placement, minimally a full-form PASSporT attesting the caller, the callee and the time of the call. Anyone could run one: a carrier, an enterprise PBX, or even a smartphone. The RFC mandates neither who operates a CPS nor how to find one.

Two dataflows are considered. In the first, the callee registers with the CPS, which pushes PASSporTs to it. That needs a full-time connection from the callee, which is costly especially for mobile devices. The RFC therefore focuses on the second: the caller stores the PASSporT, the incoming PSTN call acts as the notification, and the callee then fetches the PASSporT.

The use cases show who does the storing and fetching: an originating authentication service, an enterprise PBX, a gateway that extracts a PASSporT from a SIP request, a gateway that retrieves one and adds an Identity header, a mobile handset, or a high-volume call center.
sections.plainLanguage: The pickup point is like a locker. The caller drops a note in the locker labeled with your number, then calls you. When the phone rings, you check the locker to see that the note matches.

sections.title: How a Call Is Verified
sections.content:
Alice stores an encrypted PASSporT at the CPS under Bob's number, then places the call. Bob's phone shows the number as usual but also asks the CPS for any current PASSporTs for his number. If it can decrypt one with his private key and validate it, the phone can present the calling number as verified. Otherwise the call is unverifiable, which does not mean it is bogus, since many legitimate calls will be unverifiable during incremental deployment.

The authentication service follows steps like those of RFC 8224: confirm it can sign for the originating identity, find the destination's public encryption key and CPS, build the PASSporT (using iat, orig and dest claims), encrypt it once per discovered key, and store it before the call starts. The copy stored at the CPS MUST always be a full-form PASSporT.

The verification service fetches all PASSporTs for its number, decrypts them, drops unsupported ppt extensions and ones whose orig does not match the presented number, checks the credentials and the trust in the issuing certificate authority, checks the iat freshness, and finally verifies the signature.
sections.plainLanguage: When the phone rings, your phone quietly checks the locker. If there is a note with the caller's name, written so only you can read it, your phone tells you the caller is real.

sections.title: Encryption, Privacy and Dummy Entries
sections.content:
A design goal is that out-of-band delivery should not be worse for privacy than in-band STIR. PASSporTs are therefore encrypted with a public key tied to the called number, so any entity may retrieve them but only the key holder can read them. The CPS cannot see the contents, which makes it a less attractive target for pervasive monitoring.

Two details protect against leaks. The CPS MUST return at least one unique, plausible encrypted response to every retrieval request, even when no call is in progress, and these dummy PASSporTs MUST NOT be repeated for later calls. Callees may also ask for PASSporTs for numbers they do not own, or for a range, to hide from the CPS which numbers they control.

Encryption means a separate key lookup is needed, because the ECDSA signing key is not suitable for encryption. The RFC leaves key discovery and CPS discovery open, listing options such as provisioned locations, entries in credentials, ENUM and RELOAD. It calls the best point in the privacy versus timeliness trade-off an open issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything in the locker is in a secret code only the right person can read. The locker also hands out look-alike fake notes, so nobody can tell from outside whether a real call is happening.

sections.title: Attacks and Flood Control
sections.content:
The main attack to prevent is convincing a callee that a call is from someone else. Fake PASSporTs should fail because they must be signed by an authority for the number. Using TLS on the originating side when storing at the CPS is RECOMMENDED.

One weakness is the substitution attack. A PASSporT at the CPS shows only that Alice is trying to call Bob, not that a particular incoming call is from Alice. With a callback service, an attacker can trigger a legitimate stored PASSporT and race it with a call using forged caller ID. The RFC says in-band STIR has a similar exposure, and shortening how long PASSporTs are kept makes the attack harder. A CPS SHOULD NOT keep a PASSporT longer than the recommended iat freshness policy of sixty seconds, unless local policy says otherwise.

Because anyone may store PASSporTs, an attacker could flood the CPS with bogus ones. The proposed flood control uses blind signatures: a sender authenticates once and gets a signed token for a temporary key, then later stores anonymously, so the CPS can rate limit without learning who is calling whom. Verifiable oblivious pseudorandom functions are named as a possible faster alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could set up a fake call at the same moment as a real one. To keep the lockers from being buried in junk, each person gets a few special unmarked tickets, so the locker keeper can count them without knowing whose they are.
